name: Jade Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage High Carrow, a hill farm owned by a land trust, with eleven hundred ewes on about two thousand hectares of rough grazing that goes up to the ridge. In November the rams are in with the ewes, so I'm out on the quad bike at first light checking the raddle marks, the coloured crayon on the ram's chest that shows which ewes he's covered. I've got one full-time shepherd, Callum, and two dogs who do more work than both of us. By lunch I'm usually soaked and eating a sandwich in the bike shed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the gather, bringing the whole hill down with the dogs in September, when you come over the brow and see a thousand sheep pouring down like milk. What wears me out is the money. The trust pays me fairly for a shepherd but not for a manager, and lamb prices go up and down like the weather. We've got under a month saved, which in a valley with one shop and no other jobs feels thinner than it sounds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much technology do you use up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people think. Every ewe has an electronic ear tag, so I scan them in the race and the records go straight to my phone. I use an AI tool every day to plan grazing, write up the trust reports and sometimes just to argue with about the weather forecast. Last spring I borrowed a drone to look for ewes stuck in the bracken. I'd buy one tomorrow if I had the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. At the mart I'd show the older lads how I use it for the records, and most of them would say, very nice, Jade, and go back to their notebooks. That's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a small win for me. It saves me paperwork, and the paperwork on a hill farm is mad, every grant has three forms. It doesn't change the lamb price or the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get the trust to pay for a drone, about two thousand, by showing them the hours it saves at lambing. I'd use the AI to write the case for it. And I'd keep doing the rest the way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. Like a day when the forecast is right for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the valley has no other jobs. What would you do if High Carrow ever stopped needing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move, probably. And that's the bit I don't like thinking about. Rosa's settled at the little school, Owen does the delivery van round for the whole valley, and the cottage comes with the job. If the job goes, the house goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did you grow up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm a lowland girl, from a dairy farm. I came up for a summer job at twenty-two and never left. The old shepherd here, Duncan, told me I'd last a winter. I've done twenty-one.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and tell anyone who'd listen. At the mart I'd show the older farmers how I use it for records, even if most went back to their notebooks.
S0.think: I think it's a small win, cutting the heavy paperwork on a hill farm where every grant has three forms. It doesn't change the lamb price or the rain.
S0.do: Uses AI to write a case asking the trust to fund a drone, costing about two thousand, to save hours at lambing. Otherwise carries on as now.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, like a day when the forecast is right.
S0.quote: The old shepherd here, Duncan, told me I'd last a winter. I've done twenty-one.
S0.fieldNote: She is enthusiastic about tools and already uses AI daily, but her real vulnerability is the tied cottage: if the job goes, the house goes. That surfaced quickly when I asked about leaving. She tells her story with pride and humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good, it gives places like this a chance to catch up. But I'd also say hiring fewer beginners is short-sighted. Hill shepherding is learned on the hill, you can't do it from a book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this one helps me. The trust's office would get leaner, and I'd be doing more of the planning myself with the tools, which I like. The risk is the trust deciding to merge Carrow with the next farm and have one manager for both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it. I'd put a plan to the trust in the first six months showing how I could run both farms with the tools and one extra shepherd, and ask for a manager's wage for it. If somebody's going to run two farms, it should be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of fight in it. Like going into the sale ring with good lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running two farms is a big jump. What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the hands-on work, which I'd miss. I'd be on the laptop more and the hill less. And Callum would get the gather, which he'd love, and I'd be a bit jealous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said beginners can't learn from a book. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's apprentice, if he ever gets one. The trust only took him on because I fought for it. If they think the tools can cover it, there won't be a next Callum, and in twenty years nobody will know how to read a hill.

S1.say: I'd say slow is good because it lets places like this catch up. But hiring fewer beginners is short-sighted, since hill shepherding is learned on the hill, not from a book.
S1.think: I think it helps me, as the trust's office would shrink and I'd do more planning with tools, which I enjoy. The risk is the trust merging Carrow with the next farm under one manager.
S1.do: Puts a plan to the trust within six months to run both farms with AI tools and one extra shepherd, asking for a proper manager's wage. Aims to be the one chosen if farms are merged.
S1.feel: Calm with some fight in her, like entering the sale ring with good lambs.
S1.quote: If they think the tools can cover it, there won't be a next Callum, and in twenty years nobody will know how to read a hill.
S1.fieldNote: She turned a risk into a bid for more responsibility, which fits her adaptive streak. She did admit she'd lose the hands-on work she loves. Her centre view comes through as practical concern for training rather than politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both camps are making a racket and the answer's probably in the middle: help people retrain, and make sure the AI firms pay their share without killing them off. I'd say it at the mart and on the valley's group chat, and I'd get shouted at from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trust's head office in the city would shrink a lot, and that could be good or bad. Good if they leave more decisions to me. Bad if the person who knows me and fights for the grazing budget gets replaced by a system that just sees cost per ewe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a relationship with whoever's left at head office, early. I'd send them a monthly report I'd write with the AI, short and clear, with photos from the hill, so they see the place as more than a spreadsheet. And I'd look into one of those new AI jobs, maybe advising hill farms on using the tools, a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Advising other farms a day a week, would you have time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in lambing, no. But November to February, yes, maybe. It'd bring in a few hundred a month, which is the difference between saving something and saving nothing. Owen would say I'm doing too much, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at head office knows you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, the land agent. She's been coming up for fifteen years and she knows the ewes by their faces nearly as well as I do. If they replace her with a system, I'd lose my best ally, and I'd have to start again with a machine.

S2.say: I'd say both camps are making a racket and the answer is probably in the middle: retraining help, and AI firms paying their share without being killed off. I'd say it at the mart and on the valley chat.
S2.think: I think the trust's head office would shrink, which could mean more freedom for me. Or the person who fights for my grazing budget gets replaced by a system that only sees cost per ewe.
S2.do: Builds early ties with remaining head office staff through a short monthly AI-assisted report with photos. Looks into advising other hill farms on AI tools one day a week in winter for a few hundred a month.
S2.feel: A bit uneasy, watching the post but not scared.
S2.quote: If they replace her with a system, I'd lose my best ally, and I'd have to start again with a machine.
S2.fieldNote: She sees both a chance and a risk in the same change and plans for both. Her centre politics are almost exactly the middle ground, and she expects flak from both sides. Margaret, the land agent, is the person whose loss would really hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, but by sensible people, not by whoever shouts loudest. Some tax on the big winners, some help for the losers, and keep the lights on. I'd be one of the few in the valley who'd say that out loud, because most are either very red or very blue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in an odd spot. My job's physical, so it's fine. But the trust lives off investments, and if share prices boom, they're richer, which might mean more money for the hill. On the other hand, rich city folk buying up holiday cottages in the valley, with house prices booming, that's a problem for the school and the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the trust for a proper contract and a pay rise while they're flush, in the first quarter, with the numbers to back it. I'd also put a bit into the valley's community housing scheme, which wants to buy two cottages for local families. And I'd keep the drone and the tools, since the trust would have money for them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a sense that this is the moment to ask for things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rich city folk buying cottages. Has that already started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two went last year. One's empty eleven months of the year. The school's down to nineteen children, and if it drops below fifteen the council will close it, and then Rosa and Finn are on a bus for forty minutes each way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put money into the housing scheme, with under a month saved. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty a month, maybe. It's not a lot, but it's a vote for the valley. Owen thinks we'd be better saving it. He's probably right, and I'd do it anyway.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared by sensible people, not the loudest, with some tax on big winners and help for losers. I'd be one of the few in the valley saying that out loud.
S3.think: I think I'm in an odd spot: my physical job is safe and the trust gets richer, which may help the hill. But booming house prices bring holiday cottage buyers who threaten the school and shop.
S3.do: Asks the trust in the first quarter for a proper contract and a pay rise backed by numbers, pays about fifty a month into the valley's community housing scheme, and secures funding for the drone and tools.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a sense that this is the moment to ask for things.
S3.quote: One's empty eleven months of the year.
S3.fieldNote: She sees the boom as both a threat to her valley and a chance to bargain with a richer employer. The school numbers were a precise, telling detail. She'd spend money she can't really spare on the housing scheme and knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are coming and we should shape them, not just fear them. I'd say farm robots should be rented through co-ops or trusts, so small farms aren't squeezed out. And I'd say the hill is going to be the last place they work well, and I'd be half right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the hill buys me time, three or four years maybe, because robots struggle on steep wet ground and bracken. But there are already collars that keep sheep in with sound, no fences, and drones that gather. Put those together and the trust needs a shepherd for the hard days only. And Owen's van round, that's gone the first year, robots or drones delivering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get trained on the drones and the collars before anyone else in the valley, and offer to run them for the trust and the neighbours. I'd tell Owen to look at the care home in town, though the card says robots go there too, so maybe not. I'd want us to save two months by the end of the year, which means no holiday, and selling my old quad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd rather be anxious and moving than frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the one running the drones that replace a shepherd. How would Callum feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd feel I'd sold him out. And I'd tell him to learn it with me, so we're both the people who run it, not the people who get run over. Whether he would, I don't know. He's thirty and he hates his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most if the gather was done by drones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dogs, honestly. Moss and Bree. A drone doesn't come and lie on your feet at the end of the day. I'd keep them anyway, even if they had nothing to do.

S4.say: I'd say robots are coming and we should shape them, not just fear them, renting them through co-ops or trusts so small farms survive. I'd say the hill will be the last place they work well.
S4.think: I think the hill buys me three or four years because robots struggle on steep wet ground. But sound collars and gathering drones would mean a shepherd only for hard days, and my partner's van round would go in the first year.
S4.do: Trains on drones and virtual-fence collars before anyone else in the valley and offers to run them for the trust and neighbours. Aims to save two months of costs by year end by skipping a holiday and selling her old quad.
S4.feel: Anxious, but she'd rather be anxious and moving than frozen.
S4.quote: A drone doesn't come and lie on your feet at the end of the day.
S4.fieldNote: Even here she stays in motion, aiming to be the person who runs the machines. She knows this could hurt her colleague and her partner, and she doesn't pretend otherwise. The dogs were where her feelings showed most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, but more for Owen than for me. I can see a way through for me, I can't see one for him. What would help is cheap access to the new kit for small farms, through co-ops, and real training for people like Owen while they're still earning, not after they've lost it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the places, not just the jobs. If a valley loses its shop, its school and its shepherds, it doesn't matter how clever the robots are, there's nobody left to live there. That's what I'd want people in the cities to understand.

headlineQuote: I'd tell him to learn it with me, so we're both the people who run it, not the people who get run over.
portrait: Jade Dubois, 43, manages a hill sheep farm of eleven hundred ewes for a land trust, living in a tied cottage in a remote valley with her partner and two children and less than a month saved. She uses AI and electronic tags every day and wants a drone badly. She sees most scenarios as both threat and opening, and her instinct is always to move first: bid to run two farms, cultivate head office, train on drones and collars. Her worries are her colleague, her partner's delivery round, and her valley's school and shop rather than her own job.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, mostly because she can see a way through for herself but not for her partner, whose delivery van round would go first.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap access to new kit for small farms through co-ops, and real training for people like her partner while they're still earning.
